title: Celsus admits what Christians say of oracles
source_text: Πολλὰ δὲ Κέλσος ἐν τοῖς πρὸ τούτων εἰπὼν. μέχρι χρηστηρίων καὶ ἐπὶ τὰ μαντεῖα αὐτῶν ἀναπέμψας ἡμᾶς ὡς θεῶν. νῦν κρεῖττον πεποίηκεν ὁμολογήσας ὅτι οἱ μέλλουσαν τύχην ἀνθρώπῳ καὶ πόλει προλέγοντες καὶ ὅσοι περὶ τὰς θνητὰς πράξεις περίγειοι δαίμονές εἰσι, γενέσει συντετηκότες καὶ προσηλωμένοι αἵματι καὶ κνίσσῃ καὶ μελῳδίαις καὶ ἄλλοις τισὶ τοιούτοις προσδεδεμένοι, κρεῖττον τούτων οὐδὲν δυνάμενοι. καὶ εἰκὸς ὅτι. ἡνίκα ἱστάμεθα πρὸς Κέλσον, θεολογοῦντα τὰ χρηστήρια καὶ τὰς παρὰ τοῖς νομιζομένοις θεοῖς θεραπείας, ἀσεβεῖς τις ἡμᾶς ὑπελάμβανε, τοὺς λέγοντας δαιμόνων εἶναι ταῦτ᾿ ἔργα. κατασπώντων εἰς τὰ γενέσεως πράγματα τὰς τῶν ἀνθρώπων ψυχάς· ἀλλὰ νῦν ὁ ἐκεῖνα περὶ ἡμῶν ὑπολαβὼν πειθέσθω καλῶς λεγομένοις τοῖς ὑπὸ Χριστιανῶν καταγγελλομένοις, ὁρῶν ὅτι καὶ ὁ κατὰ Χριστιανῶν γράφων ταῦτα νῦν ἐπὶ τέλει ὡσπερεὶ νικώμενος ὑπὸ τοῦ τῆς ἀληθείας πνεύματος ἀνέγραψε. κἂν λέγῃ οὖν Κέλσος τούτοις ἀφοσιωτέον, ἐφ᾿ ὅσον συμφέρει, πάντῃ γὰρ τοῦτο ποιεῖν οὐχ αἱρεῖ λόγος· οὐκ ἀφοσιωτέον δαιμονίοις. συντετηκόσι κνίσσαις καὶ αἵμασιν, οὔτε τὸ θεῖον ὅσον ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν μολυντέον, κατάγουσιν αὐτὸ ἐπὶ μοχθηροὺς δαίμονας. εἰ δ᾿ ἠκριβώκει Κέλσος τὴν τοῦ συμφέροντος ἔννοιαν καὶ ἑωράκει ὅτι τὸ κυρίως συμφέρον ἀρετή ἐστι καὶ ἡ κατ᾿ ἀρετὴν πρᾶξις, οὐκ ἂν τὸ ἐφ᾿ ὅσον συμφέρει ἔταξεν ἐπὶ τῶν τοιῶνδε καὶ, ὡς αὐτὸς ὡμολόγησε, δαιμόνων. ἡμεῖς οὖν αἱρούμεθα. εἰ μέλλει διὰ θεραπείας τοιούτων δαιμόνων ἡ ὑγίεια ἡμῖν παραγίνεσθαι καὶ ἡ ἐν βιωτικοῖς εὐτυχία, νοσεῖν μᾶλλον καὶ ἐν βιωτικοῖς δυστυχεῖν μετὰ συνειδότος τοῦ πρὸς τὸν θεὸν τῶν ὅλων καθαρῶς εὐσεβοῦς, ἤπερ μετὰ τοῦ σχίζεσθαι καὶ ἀποπίπτειν τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ τὴν ψυχὴν ἐσχάτως νοσεῖν καὶ κακοδαιμονεῖν ὑγιαίνειν τῷ σώματι καὶ ἐν βιωτικοῖς ἀπαλλάσσειν εὐτυχέστερον· καὶ τῷ ἀπροσδεεῖ γε παντὸς οὑτινοσοῦν πλὴν τῆς ἀνθρώπων σωτηρίας καὶ παντὸς λογικοῦ προσελθετέον. ἢ τοῖς χρῄζουσι κνίσσης καὶ αἵματος.
pass_a_gloss: Celsus, having said many things in the things before these, as far as oracles (χρηστήρια), and having sent us up (ἀναπέμπω) to their oracle-shrines (μαντεῖα) as of gods, now has done better (κρεῖττον ποιέω), confessing (ὁμολογέω) that those foretelling coming fortune to man and city, and as many as are about mortal actions, are earthly demons, melted into generation and nailed to blood and savour and melodies and bound to other such things, able to do nothing better than these. And it is likely that, when we stood (ἵσταμαι) against Celsus theologizing (θεολογέω) the oracles and the services among the supposed gods (νομιζόμενοι θεοί), someone supposed (ὑπολαμβάνω) us impious (ἀσεβεῖς), saying that these are works (ἔργα) of demons dragging down (κατασπάω) the souls of men into the affairs of generation; but now let the one who supposed those things about us be persuaded (πείθομαι) by the things proclaimed (καταγγέλλω) by Christians as well said, seeing that even the one writing against Christians now at the end (ἐπὶ τέλει) wrote these things, as if conquered (νικάω) by the spirit of truth (πνεῦμα τῆς ἀληθείας). And if Celsus says: to these one must discharge religious duty (ἀφοσιωτέον) so far as it benefits (συμφέρει), for reason (λόγος) does not establish (αἱρέω) doing this in every way; one must not discharge religious duty to demons melted into savours and bloods, nor must the divine (τὸ θεῖον) as far as in us be defiled (μολυντέον), bringing it down to wicked (μοχθηροί) demons. If Celsus had examined exactly (ἀκριβόω) the notion (ἔννοια) of the beneficial (τὸ συμφέρον) and seen that the properly (κυρίως) beneficial is virtue (ἀρετή) and the action according to virtue, he would not have placed (τάσσω) 'so far as it benefits' about such beings and, as he himself confessed, demons. We therefore choose (αἱρέομαι), if through the service of such demons health (ὑγίεια) and good fortune in matters of life (βιωτικά) will come to us, rather to be sick and unfortunate in matters of life with a conscience (συνειδός) purely (καθαρῶς) pious toward the God of the universe, than with being split off (σχίζομαι) and falling away (ἀποπίπτω) from God and being extremely (ἐσχάτως) sick in soul and wretched (κακοδαιμονέω) to be healthy in the body and to fare (ἀπαλλάσσω) more fortunately in matters of life; and to the one lacking nothing (ἀπροσδεής) whatever except the salvation (σωτηρία) of men and of every rational being one must approach (προσελθετέον), rather than to those needing savour and blood.
pass_b_english: Earlier Celsus said a great deal, going so far as to speak of oracles and to send us off to their oracular shrines as though to gods. Now he has done better, admitting that those who foretell the coming fortune of a man and of a city, and all who are concerned with mortal affairs, are earthly demons, fused with the world of becoming, nailed to blood and the smoke of sacrifice and to songs, and bound to other such things, and able to do nothing better than these.

And it is likely that, when we were standing against Celsus as he treated the oracles and the worship given to the supposed gods as divine, someone took us for impious, because we said that these were the works of demons who drag the souls of men down to the affairs of the world of becoming. But now let the one who formed that opinion of us be persuaded that what Christians proclaim is well said, seeing that even the man who writes against Christians has now, at the end, put this in writing, as though overcome by the Spirit of truth (John 14:17).

So even if Celsus says: “We must pay these their due rites, so far as it is to our advantage, for reason does not justify doing this in every respect,” we must not pay due rites to demons that are fused with the smoke of sacrifice and with blood, nor must we, for our part, defile the divine by dragging it down to wicked demons. If Celsus had examined the idea of advantage with care and had seen that what is advantage in the proper sense is virtue and action in keeping with virtue, he would not have set down “so far as it is to our advantage” in the case of beings like these, who are, as he himself admitted, demons.

We therefore choose, if health and good fortune in the affairs of life are to come to us through the worship of such demons, rather to be sick and to be unfortunate in the affairs of life, with a conscience that is purely reverent toward the God of all, than to be healthy in body and to fare more fortunately in the affairs of life while being cut off and falling away from God and being sick in soul to the last degree and wretched. We must draw near to Him who needs nothing at all except the salvation of men and of every rational being, rather than to those who crave the smoke of sacrifice and blood.

choices.choice: τοῦ τῆς ἀληθείας πνεύματος is the Johannine title ‘the Spirit of truth’ (John 14:17; also 15:26; 16:13); cited at John 14:17 as an allusion of phrase, with Spirit capitalised, though Origen’s ‘as though’ (ὡσπερεί) makes the image rhetorical; a reviewer may lower the capital and drop the citation if the phrase is judged not an allusion. Celsus’s words ‘We must pay these their due rites ... in every respect’ are quoted; Origen’s reply begins ‘we must not pay’. ἀφοσιωτέον rendered ‘pay due rites’ (discharge a religious obligation). θεολογοῦντα rendered ‘treated ... as divine’. κακοδαιμονεῖν (‘be wretched’, literally ‘have an evil daemon’) carries a pun the English cannot keep. Koetschau’s stops after εἰπών, εἰκὸς ὅτι, ἔργα, δαιμονίοις, αἱρούμεθα and προσελθετέον are read as pauses inside sentences. No direct Scripture quotation. Review: the John 14:17 allusion is kept; the word order τοῦ τῆς ἀληθείας πνεύματος reproduces the Johannine title, and Origen uses the same image of Celsus overcome by truth elsewhere. τῷ ἀπροσδεεῖ (God needing nothing) may recall Acts 17:25, but it is also a philosophical commonplace, so it is not cited.
οὐχ αἱρεῖ λόγος 'does not require' to 'does not justify' (reason does not establish it)
ἐπὶ τῶν τοιῶνδε καὶ ... δαιμόνων: καί read as identifying, 'beings like these, who are, as he himself admitted, demons'
John 14:17 'Spirit of truth' checked against the verse and kept
